claim: Lambda can send records of asynchronous invocations to a standard SQS queue, a standard SNS topic, an Amazon S3 bucket (on failure only), a Lambda function, or an EventBridge event bus.
question: Which AWS services can be a destination for records of asynchronous Lambda invocations?

values.display: An Amazon S3 bucket (on failure only)

qualifiers.condition: an S3 bucket only for failed invocations

evidence.quote: Lambda can send records of asynchronous invocations to one of the following AWS services. Amazon SQS – A standard SQS queue Amazon SNS – A standard SNS topic Amazon S3 – An Amazon S3 bucket (on failure only) AWS Lambda – A Lambda function Amazon EventBridge – An EventBridge event bus

claim: An Amazon SQS FIFO queue or an Amazon SNS FIFO topic is an unsupported destination type for asynchronous invocation records; when Lambda cannot send a record to a configured destination, it sends a DestinationDeliveryFailures metric to Amazon CloudWatch.
question: Can an SQS FIFO queue or SNS FIFO topic be a destination for asynchronous invocation records?

values.spoken: FIFO queues and FIFO topics are not supported

evidence.quote: If Lambda can't send a record to a destination you have configured, it sends a DestinationDeliveryFailures metric to Amazon CloudWatch. This can happen if your configuration includes an unsupported destination type, such as an Amazon SQS FIFO queue or an Amazon SNS FIFO topic.

claim: You can configure separate destinations for successfully processed events and for events that fail all processing attempts; alternatively, a standard SQS queue or standard SNS topic can be a dead-letter queue for discarded events, and Lambda sends a dead-letter queue only the content of the event, without details about the response.
question: How does a dead-letter queue differ from an on-failure destination for asynchronous invocations?

values.spoken: destinations for success and for failure

values.display: a dead-letter queue for discarded events
only sends the content of the event

evidence.quote: You can configure separate destinations for events that are processed successfully, and events that fail all processing attempts. Alternatively, you can configure a standard Amazon SQS queue or standard Amazon SNS topic as a dead-letter queue for discarded events. For dead-letter queues, Lambda only sends the content of the event, without details about the response.

claim: When reserved concurrency is set to zero for an asynchronously invoked function, Lambda begins sending new events to the configured dead-letter queue or on-failure destination without any retries.
question: What happens to new asynchronous events when a function's reserved concurrency is set to zero?

qualifiers.condition: a dead-letter queue or on-failure destination is configured

evidence.quote: When you set reserved concurrency to zero for an asynchronously invoked function, Lambda begins sending new events to the configured dead-letter queue or the on-failure event destination, without any retries.

claim: A function can have multiple destinations, so successful and failed events can go to separate destinations, and destinations can be configured on a function, a function version or an alias.
question: Can destinations be set per version or alias, and can success and failure go to different targets?

values.display: Each function can have multiple destinations
values.spoken: a function can have several destinations

evidence.quote: Each function can have multiple destinations, so you can configure separate destinations for successful and failed events. Each record sent to the destination is a JSON document with details about the invocation. Like error handling settings, you can configure destinations on an Event Function, function version, or alias.

claim: By default an event source mapping can have up to 5 filters, which are logically ORed; a record that satisfies none of them is discarded by Lambda and not sent to the function. A quota increase allows up to 10 filters for each event source.
question: How many filters can an event source mapping have, and what happens to a record that matches none of them?

values.spoken: up to ten with a quota increase

qualifiers.condition: a quota increase allows up to 10 filters for each event source

evidence.quote: By default, you can define up to five different filters for a single event source mapping. Your filters are logically ORed together. If a record from your event source satisfies one or more of your filters, Lambda includes the record in the next event it sends to your function. If none of your filters are satisfied, Lambda discards the record.
If you need to define more than five filters for an event source, you can request a quota increase for up to 10 filters for each event source.

claim: Event filtering works only with certain event source mappings, and Lambda does not support event filtering for Amazon DocumentDB.
question: Does Lambda event filtering work with every event source mapping?

values.display: works only with certain event source mappings
values.spoken: filtering works only with some event source mappings

values.display: doesn't support event filtering for Amazon DocumentDB

evidence.quote: Event filtering works only with certain event source mappings.
Lambda doesn't support event filtering for Amazon DocumentDB.

claim: For an Amazon SQS event source, if a message does not satisfy the filter criteria, Lambda automatically removes the message from the queue, so you do not delete it manually.
question: What happens to an SQS message that does not match an event source mapping's filter?

values.display: automatically removes the message from the queue
values.spoken: Lambda deletes it from the queue for you

values.display: You don't have to manually delete these messages

qualifiers.scope: Amazon SQS event source mapping with filters

evidence.quote: For Amazon SQS, if a message doesn't satisfy your filter criteria, Lambda automatically removes the message from the queue. You don't have to manually delete these messages in Amazon SQS.

claim: If a function is invoked approximately 16 times in the same chain of requests, Lambda automatically stops the next function invocation in that chain and notifies you; invocations from the function's other triggers are not affected.
question: When does Lambda recursive loop detection stop a function?

values.display: automatically stops the next function invocation

qualifiers.condition: recursive loop detection turned on (the default)

evidence.quote: If your function is invoked approximately 16 times in the same chain of requests, then Lambda automatically stops the next function invocation in that request chain and notifies you. If your function is configured with multiple triggers, then invocations from other triggers aren't affected.

claim: Recursive loop detection is turned on by default for all AWS customers, costs nothing, and does not need X-Ray active tracing; by default, when Lambda detects a recursive loop it stops the function being invoked and notifies you, and a function that is recursive by design can be configured to allow recursive invocation.
question: Is Lambda recursive loop detection on by default, does it cost anything, and can it be turned off?

values.display: turned on by default for all AWS customers
There is no charge to use the feature
allow it to be invoked recursively

qualifiers.condition: a function can be configured to allow recursive invocation

evidence.quote: You don't need to enable X-Ray active tracing for this feature to work. Recursive loop detection is turned on by default for all AWS customers. There is no charge to use the feature.

By default, when Lambda detects a recursive loop, it stops your function being invoked and notifies you. If your design intentionally uses recursive patterns, you can a change a function's default configuration to allow it to be invoked recursively.

claim: Lambda can detect only recursive loops that include certain supported services, and the function must use a supported AWS SDK; it currently detects loops between functions, Amazon SQS, Amazon S3, Amazon SNS and Amazon EventBridge custom event buses, and loops made only of Lambda functions.
question: Which services does Lambda recursive loop detection cover?

values.display: Amazon SQS, Amazon S3, Amazon SNS
values.spoken: SQS, S3, SNS and EventBridge custom event buses

values.display: use one of the supported AWS SDKs

qualifiers.condition: the function uses a supported AWS SDK

evidence.quote: Lambda can detect only recursive loops that include certain supported AWS services. For recursive loops to be detected, your function must also use one of the supported AWS SDKs.

Lambda currently detects recursive loops between your functions, Amazon SQS, Amazon S3, Amazon SNS, and Amazon EventBridge Custom event buses. Lambda also detects loops comprised only of Lambda functions, which might invoke each other synchronously or asynchronously.

claim: Unintentional recursive loops can bill unexpected charges to your account and can make Lambda scale and use all of the account's available concurrency.
question: Why are recursive loops between Lambda and another service dangerous?

values.display: unexpected charges being billed to your AWS account
use all of your account's available concurrency

evidence.quote: Unintentional recursive loops can result in unexpected charges being billed to your AWS account. Loops can also cause Lambda to scale and use all of your account's available concurrency.
